title: Probability, Biostatistics & Experimental Design
description: Probability, estimation, hypothesis testing, regression, and design principles for biological and engineering experiments, with reproducibility and uncertainty at the center.

modifications: Expanded week 1 with event and conditional-probability definitions, Bayes' rule and a synthetic diagnostic-count example, discrete distributions, sampling distributions, standard-error calculations, independence and experimental-unit checks, and model limits. Clarified both objectives and mapped them and the practice assessment to outcomes 1 and 6. Reassociated the preserved standard-error check to the sampling-variability objective and added one Bayes calculation so both objectives have direct practice evidence. Added an MIT OpenCourseWare 18.05 Reading 3 page as a link-only technical reference.

Expanded week 4 with repeated-sampling coverage, a paired-mean t interval calculation, precision versus magnitude, practical thresholds, effect-size scales, bias limits, and regression to the mean. Mapped both existing objectives and the unchanged practice assessment to outcome 3; the interval and effect-size question prompts and keys remain unchanged. Added MIT OpenCourseWare 18.05 Reading 23a as a link-only reference.

Expanded week 6 with null and alternative hypotheses, conditional p-value interpretation, Type I and II error, power, analysis-plan dependence, family-wise error, Bonferroni control, and confirmatory versus exploratory distinctions. Mapped both objectives and the formative assessment to outcomes 2 and 3. Corrected the two preserved multiplicity items to the multiplicity objective and added one p-value interpretation item so both objectives have direct practice evidence. Added MIT OpenCourseWare 18.05 NHST II and Problem Set 9 Solutions as link-only references.

Expanded week 8 with assignment and observational units, randomization, blocking, replication levels, regression models for treatment and nuisance factors, residual diagnostics, and reproducible analysis. Mapped both objectives and the practice assessment to outcomes 1, 2 and 4. Corrected the preserved sample-size question's objective association and added a blocked-randomization item so both objectives have direct practice evidence. Added MIT OpenCourseWare Reading 26 and an open PLOS Biology paper on experimental units as link-only references.

The MIT 18.05 Spring 2022 calendar and Reading 15 are link-only curriculum and technical references; no source asset or assessment was imported. outcomes.description: Distinguish sampling variability from measurement error.
Choose an analysis matched to design and outcome.
Interpret confidence intervals, p-values, and effect sizes.
Design controls, replication, randomization, and blinding.
Create a labeled quantitative graph using an explicit scale and the units of the measured variables.
Use conditional probability and Bayes' rule to update an event probability from evidence.
Update a finite prior over model parameters with likelihoods, normalize a posterior, and compute posterior predictive probabilities distinct from p-values.
Update a continuous Beta prior with binomial observations and compute posterior predictive probabilities under stated assumptions.
Derive supported joint, marginal and conditional laws and verify covariance and total-variance relationships.
Construct a likelihood from observed data and exposure, solve selected maximum-likelihood estimates and qualify curvature and boundary conclusions.
Update a normal mean with known observation variance and distinguish posterior, predictive and shared-parameter uncertainty.
Fit and diagnose a multiple linear model, verify rank and residual structure and distinguish mean-response from new-observation uncertainty.

lesson_objectives.description: Apply conditional probability and Bayes' rule to update an event probability from evidence.
Explain how a sample mean varies across repeated independent samples and how its standard error describes that sampling variability.
Interpret an interval as a procedure for repeated sampling.
Separate magnitude from statistical precision.
Interpret p-values conditional on the null and analysis plan.
Account for multiplicity and distinguish confirmatory from exploratory work.
Use randomization and blocking to reduce confounding.
Assess model residuals and distinguish replication levels.
Distinguish an observed descriptive mean difference from evidence of a causal or population-level effect.
Calculate group sample means from replicate values and place their coordinates on a labeled linear graph.
Compute a Kaplan-Meier survival estimate at a stated time from event and censoring times.
Explain why censored observations must not be dropped or treated as events.
Compare two groups with an event rate per person-time and interpret a rate ratio and its limits as an estimate of a hazard ratio.
Calculate the family-wise error rate and the expected number of false positives across many independent tests.
Apply the Bonferroni correction and the Benjamini–Hochberg procedure to a list of p-values and count the rejections each allows.
Choose between family-wise and false-discovery control for a study goal, and interpret an adjusted result correctly.
Compute a difference in means, its standard error and a 95% confidence interval, and interpret the interval.
Calculate a standardized effect size and explain how sample size changes precision but not the effect.
Predict the expected remeasurement of an extreme value under regression to the mean and evaluate study designs that guard against it.
Distinguish biological variation from technical (measurement) error and estimate the technical error from replicate measurements.
Compute the standard error of a mean for nested data, the intraclass correlation and the effective sample size.
Evaluate how replication should be allocated between independent biological units and repeated measurements, and what a naive analysis overstates.
Compute the standard error, t statistic and Welch degrees of freedom for a difference between two independent group means.
Construct and interpret a confidence interval for the difference and a standardized effect size.
Choose between independent-groups and paired analyses, and compute a paired t statistic.
Compute the signal-to-noise ratio, the approximate power and the sample size per group for a two-group comparison.
Show how the required sample size scales with the effect size and the variability.
Evaluate a small study's results, including the smallest significant difference and the exaggeration of significant estimates, and state what a non-significant result does and does not show.
Compute the least-squares slope, intercept, residual standard deviation, R² and standard error of the slope from data.
Use a calibration line to estimate an unknown and describe how its uncertainty depends on the data.
Evaluate a fit using residuals, and state when R², extrapolation or causal readings of a slope are unjustified.
Carry out an exact permutation test for a difference in means and compute its p-value by counting arrangements.
Explain the logic of the bootstrap and compute simple properties of bootstrap resamples.
Compute rank sums and a Mann–Whitney statistic, and choose among t-test, permutation and rank-based analyses for a given design.
Summarize nested readings to one value per animal and identify the number of independent units in each group.
Estimate the technical variance, the between-animal variance and the intraclass correlation from nested readings.
Compare an analysis that treats readings as independent with an animal-level analysis, and state what the design supports.
Compute the positive predictive value of a diagnostic test from prevalence, sensitivity and specificity, and express the update with a likelihood ratio.
Compute the probability that a statistically significant finding is true from the prior probability of a real effect, the power and the significance level.
Evaluate what a significant result, a replication and a screening pipeline can support.
Re-analyze a pilot result with the independent unit and a correction for the number of outcomes examined.
Plan the sample size of a confirmatory study from the smallest effect of interest and the variance components, including the number of technical readings.
Specify the elements of a pre-specified confirmatory plan and state what the pilot supports and does not support.
Calculate finite-state likelihoods and normalize prior-weighted likelihoods into a posterior distribution.
Compute posterior odds and posterior predictive probabilities for a separate holdout under the stated model.
Distinguish likelihood, posterior, predictive probability and p-value, and state the assumptions each calculation uses.
Update a Beta prior after binomial observations and identify the posterior parameters.
Compute a posterior mean and integrate over posterior uncertainty for a future binomial count.
Evaluate how prior concentration and conditional exchangeability constrain interpretation and prediction.
Align randomization, analysis and sample-size units in a nested observation design.
Specify a primary contrast, target effect and analysis before observing a new outcome.
Calculate an approximate independent-unit requirement and show variance and attrition sensitivity.
Quantify a declared secondary-family threshold while keeping the primary question separate.
Create a reproducible analysis and reporting plan with accessible independent-unit displays.
Normalize a supported joint density and derive marginal means.
Compute covariance/correlation while distinguishing them from independence.
Use the event region and the conditional reference density.
Close the total-variance decomposition and bound a CLT interpretation.
Construct the correct event/exposure likelihood and maximum.
Derive observed curvature and qualify an approximate standard error.
Interpret relative likelihood and an open-domain boundary supremum.
Distinguish a maximum-likelihood summary from posterior inference.
Complete a normal posterior with explicit variance/precision units.
Distinguish future observation and future-average uncertainty.
Account for marginal predictive dependence from shared parameter uncertainty.
Construct a conditional credible interval and separate it from a coverage claim.
Solve a full-rank multiple regression from original rows.
Explain a reduced-model slope through correlated predictors.
Verify residual variance and correct residual degrees of freedom.
Separate mean-response and new-observation uncertainty and causal limits.
Derive a finite count distribution and covariance-aware variance.
Derive distinct marginal and conditional quantities from a supported density.
Enumerate finite-sample coverage and interpret a boundary bootstrap.
Enumerate a prespecified randomization tail with the correct allocation count.
Verify a distinct multiple fit through original residual equations.
Use prediction target and design information to bound a regression claim.
Integrate event/exposure, likelihood, curvature and parameter units.
Separate posterior, predictive and shared-parameter uncertainty in a cumulative report.

duration.equivalent_structure: Proposed 14-week undergraduate scope only. The four former compact prototype readings in weeks 1, 4, 6 and 8 now have expanded instruction beside original lessons on variability and pseudoreplication, comparing two groups, power, regression and calibration, resampling, base rates and replication, and planning a confirmatory study; week 12 is a synthetic-data lab on nested designs and week 14 pairs the planning lesson with the course case. All activities are open, ungraded practice. There are no graded homework sets, exams or project, and workload has not been measured, so this schedule is not evidence of semester equivalence.

lessons.title: Probability, distributions, and sampling
lessons.worked_example: Among 1,000 people at 10% prevalence, a test with 90% sensitivity and a 5% false-positive rate yields 90 true positives and 45 false positives, so P(condition|positive)=90/135=0.667. For independent measurements with s=10 and n=25, estimated SE=10/√25=2 units.

modules.title: Estimation, confidence intervals, and effect sizes

lessons.title: Estimation, confidence intervals, and effect sizes
lessons.worked_example: In a synthetic paired study, 25 independent differences average 4.0 mm with SD 2.0 mm; SE=0.40 mm, so the 95% t interval is about 4.0 ± 2.064(0.40)=[3.17,4.83] mm. It excludes zero under the model, but whether 4 mm matters depends on the prespecified threshold, measurement error, bias, and target population.

lessons.title: Hypothesis tests and multiple comparisons
lessons.worked_example: Under the global null, ten independent tests at α=0.05 have FWER 1−0.95¹⁰≈0.401. For twenty planned hypotheses, Bonferroni gives 0.05/20=0.0025 per test. The independence formula and Bonferroni bound answer different questions; neither turns a p-value into the probability that a hypothesis is true.

lessons.title: Experimental design, regression, and reproducibility
lessons.worked_example: Suppose 24 independent donor-derived samples are assigned to two conditions across four processing days. Put six samples in each day block, allocate three to each condition at random within every day, and randomize measurement order within each day. With treatment assigned to each donor-derived sample, there are 24 experimental units; measured wells and cells are nested. A treatment-plus-day model estimates the blocked comparison. If each condition occurred only on different days, treatment and day could not be separated by regression.

modules.title: Descriptive evidence and limits of inference

lessons.title: Descriptive differences and inferential limits
lessons.worked_example: At 0, 2, and 4 μM, replicate signal means of 5, 10, and 15 form the plotted sample coordinates. Plotting the means preserves the dose order but hides within-group spread; it does not establish uncertainty or causation.

lessons.title: Time-to-event data: censoring, Kaplan–Meier estimates and hazard ratios
lessons.worked_example: In the ten-subject table S(5) = 0.9 × 8/9 × 6/7 = 0.6857, S(8) = 0.5486 and the median is 10 months; 12 events in 480 person-months against 20 in 400 gives a rate ratio of 0.50.

lessons.title: Many tests at once: family-wise error, Bonferroni and the false discovery rate
lessons.worked_example: Twenty null tests at 0.05 give FWER 0.642; for ten synthetic p-values, Bonferroni at 0.005 rejects 2 while Benjamini–Hochberg at q = 0.05 rejects 4, because the fourth-smallest p (0.020) meets its threshold (4/10 × 0.05).

modules.title: Effect sizes, intervals and regression to the mean

lessons.title: Effect sizes, confidence intervals and regression to the mean: reading a result for what it can support
lessons.worked_example: A 1.5-unit difference with SE 0.949 gives a 95% interval (-0.42, 3.42) and d = 0.50; quadrupling n halves SE to 0.474; a first reading of 130 with r = 0.7 is expected to retest at 121 with no intervention.

lessons.title: Sources of variability: biological variation, technical error and the standard error
lessons.worked_example: With σ_b = 10 and σ_t = 5, four animals measured three times each have a correct standard error of 5.20, not the naive 3.23; the ICC is 0.80, the design effect 2.6 and the 12 readings are worth 4.6 independent observations; tripling the animals cuts the standard error by 42%, tripling the readings by 7%.

lessons.title: Comparing two groups: the t statistic, Welch's test, paired designs and confidence intervals for a difference
lessons.worked_example: Groups of 6 with means 10.2 and 13.0 and standard deviations 2.0 and 2.4 give SE 1.28, t = 2.20, Welch df 9.7 and p about 0.054, with a 95% interval of (−0.05, 5.65) and d = 1.27; the same mean difference in a paired design (SD of differences 1.5) gives t = 4.57, p about 0.006.

lessons.title: Power and sample size: what an experiment can detect, and what a non-significant result means
lessons.worked_example: With σ = 2.2, δ = 2.8 and 6 per group the signal-to-noise ratio is 2.20 and power about 0.51; 80% power needs 9.7 per group by the normal formula (11 exactly), and 39 if the effect is halved; with 6 per group only differences above 2.83 are significant, which exaggerates a true difference of 1.4 by at least 2.0-fold.

lessons.title: Regression and calibration: least squares, residuals, R² and prediction
lessons.worked_example: A six-point calibration gives slope 9.76, intercept 6.05, residual SD 3.21, R² 0.9939 and SE of the slope 0.384; a signal of 55 corresponds to 5.02 μM; a saturating response has R² 0.96 with curved residuals, which shows that R² does not prove linearity.

lessons.title: Resampling and rank-based methods: permutation tests, the bootstrap and the Mann–Whitney test
lessons.worked_example: Eight values in two groups of four have 70 equally likely arrangements; a fully separated split gives an exact two-sided p of 0.029, the smallest attainable with four per group; an observation appears in a bootstrap resample of size 10 with probability 0.651; the treated group's rank sum is 26 and U is 0; a less clean split (2.75) gives p = 0.20.

modules.title: Virtual laboratory: pseudoreplication and nested designs

lessons.title: Virtual lab 1: pseudoreplication and nested designs
lessons.worked_example: With four animals per group and three readings each, a reading-level t test gives t = 3.55 (p = 0.0018) while the animal-level test gives t = 1.93 (p = 0.10), because the intraclass correlation of 0.91 makes 12 readings per group worth about 4.3; the animal is the unit of analysis.

lessons.title: From p-values to evidence: base rates, positive predictive value and replication
lessons.worked_example: A test with 90% sensitivity and 95% specificity at 2% prevalence has a positive predictive value of 0.27 (LR⁺ 18); with one true hypothesis in ten, α = 0.05 and power 0.5, 0.53 of significant findings are true (0.64 at power 0.8, 0.14 if the prior is 0.01); an exact replication at the same power is significant with probability 0.29.

lessons.title: Finite Bayesian updating: priors, likelihood and prediction
lessons.worked_example: A finite prior puts probabilities 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2 on Bernoulli success rates 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8. After two successes the likelihoods are 0.04, 0.25 and 0.64, the evidence is 0.223, and the normalized posterior is 20/223, 75/223 and 128/223. The probability of exactly one success in a separate two-trial holdout is about 0.381.

modules.title: Continuous Bayesian updating and Beta–Binomial prediction

lessons.title: Continuous Bayesian updating: Beta–Binomial conjugacy and prediction
lessons.worked_example: A Beta(2,2) prior updated by eight positive and two negative results becomes Beta(10,4), with mean 5/7. Integrating that posterior gives probability 11/28 for exactly two successes in three future trials, compared with about 0.437 from plugging the mean into a binomial model.

lessons.title: Planning a confirmatory study: what a pilot with one p = 0.04 can and cannot support
lessons.worked_example: A synthetic pilot of 12 outcomes in 5 animals per group with 4 readings each and a best p of 0.03 has a 0.46 chance of at least one p below 0.05 under no effect, a Bonferroni threshold of 0.0042 (adjusted p 0.36), and 8 animal-level against 38 reading-level degrees of freedom; for the 18-marker pilot, animal-level t is 1.35 (p 0.21), a confirmatory study to detect 5.0 units needs about 51 animals per group with three readings, and 95 if all 18 markers must be confirmed with Bonferroni.

lessons.title: Confirmatory-protocol dossier project guide (optional, ungraded)
lessons.worked_example: For a separate two-arm normal approximation with target difference 2 points, sigma 3, alpha 0.05 and power 0.8, use z = 1.96 and 0.84: n = 35.28 rounds to 36 retained units per arm; a 20% attrition allowance gives 45 allocated per arm. At sigma 4, 63 retained becomes 79 allocated.

modules.title: Joint laws, conditioning and total variance

lessons.title: Joint laws, conditioning and total variance
lessons.worked_example: The triangular support has area one half and density two, giving total one. Integrating y from zero to x gives fX=two x, while integrating x from y to one gives fY=two(1−y). Their means are two thirds and one third.

lessons.title: Likelihood estimation and censored exposure
lessons.worked_example: There are two events and sixteen exposure units, so lambda_hat=two/sixteen=one/eight and estimated mean is eight. Censored records contribute survival exposure without another event factor. Dropping their durations or counting them as events changes the supplied model.

lessons.title: Normal conjugacy and shared prediction
lessons.worked_example: Prior precision is one/four and data precision three/sixteen, giving total seven/sixteen and posterior variance sixteen/seven. Multiplying by the linear coefficient four/four+eighteen/sixteen gives posterior mean thirty-four/seven. These are conditional on the supplied prior and known observation variance.

lessons.title: Multiple regression and prediction
lessons.worked_example: The original normal equations give coefficients one, two, three and residuals (one, minus one, minus two, two, one, minus one). Verify that residuals are orthogonal to every design column. That projection property does not prove independent random errors or causality. Verify the original probability, support, design and conditioning assumptions independently before interpreting this selected result.

lessons.title: Assignment 1: probability ledgers
lessons.worked_example: There are ten pairs, with counts three, six, one for K=zero, one, two. The mean is 0.8 and second moment one, giving variance 0.36. The ordered joint-marked probability is one/tenth, so covariance is 0.1−0.16=−0.06; both representations agree when denominators stay consistent. Verify the original probability, support, design and conditioning assumptions independently before interpreting this selected result.

lessons.title: Assignment 2: exact coverage and randomization
lessons.worked_example: Only k=zero and four miss one/half under the Wald rule, with total probability two/sixteen. Thus coverage is fourteen/sixteen. The exact all-failure upper endpoint solves (one−p)^four=0.025. Resampling the all-failure empirical distribution cannot repair its boundary degeneracy. Verify the original probability, support, design and conditioning assumptions independently before interpreting this selected result.

lessons.title: Assignment 3: regression and design evidence
lessons.worked_example: The coefficients are three, four, minus two and residuals (one half, minus one half, minus one, one, one half, minus one half). They are orthogonal to all three design columns and have squared sum three. The exact constructed fit does not establish a real error distribution.

lessons.title: Assignment 4: inference and prediction dossier
lessons.worked_example: Three observed events and twelve exposure units give rate one/four and mean four. Information is three/(one/four)²=48 and approximate rate SE one/sqrt48. This local approximation does not establish finite-sample coverage or correct censoring in an empirical study.

limitations: The four expanded prototype readings accompany seventeen other topic readings, four connected reports, one synthetic lab and the optional project guide; this package is not equivalent to a full university semester.

A proposed 14-week schedule exists but is unmeasured and unreviewed. There is one synthetic-data virtual lab and four open connected reports but no experimental laboratory sequence, midterm, cumulative final or graded integrative project.

Practice items remain short formative checks (two to three per expanded prototype unit and two to nine per original lesson); they do not demonstrate comprehensive outcome coverage or mastery, and objective associations remain provisional.
Bloom labels and structured prerequisite edges are initial authoring classifications awaiting subject-matter review.
Question answers and solution feedback are intentionally public practice authoring specifications, not restricted exam keys.
Total workload and weekly duration are unknown; former nominal credit values and hardcoded reading times do not establish workload.
The graph exercise checks coordinate placement on author-specified axes; it does not assess axis selection, uncertainty bars, model fitting, or interpretation.

All data, animals and numbers are synthetic teaching examples; this package gives no laboratory protocols or medical advice and says nothing about any real compound, organism or person. Sample-size calculations use normal approximations with rounded critical values unless an exact calculation is stated.

Bayesian coverage includes finite-prior, Beta–Binomial and one known-variance normal conjugate model. General unknown-variance conjugacy, broad likelihood theory and richer hierarchical/covariate inference remain outside this selected treatment.

The optional confirmatory-protocol dossier project is ungraded. Its milestone drafts are private self-checks; no software check evaluates the learner’s written derivation, diagram or interpretation. The proposed schedule and time estimate have not been measured.

Four foundations and four connected open reports deepen supported joint laws/total variance, selected censored exponential likelihood and binomial MLE, known-variance normal conjugacy, multiple-regression algebra/prediction and exact finite coverage/randomization. These selected models do not reproduce the comparator’s full probability/distribution/theory/problem-set/studio/exam sequence; measured workload and qualified review remain open.

All records and normalized tables are invented. Censoring is stipulated noninformative and parameter-independent; normal observation variance is known by assumption. Constructed least-squares residuals do not establish empirical independent normal errors. Checkpoints evaluate selected responses, not code, proofs, plots, reports, causal identification or real biological model validity.

Of the 147 numerical answers, 2 require units, 69 check significant figures and 1 check dimensions. New continuous responses request three significant figures in named reporting units; exact allocation and degree counts have no significant-figure requirement.
intentionally_omitted: Graded assessments and a laboratory sequence are not authored yet (one synthetic-data virtual lab exists); the original lessons extend a partial package.
